name: Cranberry
short: Several case reports describe raised INR in people on warfarin, but a controlled trial of moderate cranberry juice intake found no clinically important interaction.
text: Evidence on cranberry and warfarin points in two directions. Several case reports indicate that cranberry products may raise INR in people taking warfarin; one describes an 85-year-old woman whose INR rose two- to three-fold after eating cranberry sauce on two separate occasions. However, the same report's literature review found that most pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies showed no significant interaction, and a randomised double-blind trial in 30 patients on stable warfarin given 240 mL of cranberry juice or placebo daily for 2 weeks found no effect on warfarin blood levels and only a small INR difference at a single time point, which the authors judged unlikely to be clinically important. A 2021 safety review concluded that cranberry is not associated with serious adverse effects but identified warfarin interactions and kidney stone formation as potential risks. It reported that warfarin interactions were not associated with moderate juice intakes (240 to 480 mL), that some reports suggested the potential for an interaction requires excessive intakes (1 to 2 L of juice or 3000 mg of cranberry extract a day in the cited review), that cases mostly involved people with serious illnesses or taking other medicines, and that data on kidney stone formation are contradictory.
